modal.intro: Hover, focus or select a component to see what it does and how it connects.
modal.scrollHint: Scroll sideways to see the whole diagram, or open the list below.
modal.diagramLabel: Interactive diagram: {name}. Each component is a button that shows its details.

cloud1.title: Cloud-1 architecture
cloud1.description: Terraform provisions the AWS infrastructure, Ansible configures the host over SSH, and Docker Compose runs WordPress behind Nginx. Orange arrows follow a visitor's request; violet arrows show provisioning.

make.name: make up
make.description: One command runs the whole pipeline in order, each stage using what the previous one produced. make down destroys the infrastructure but keeps the Elastic IP.
facts: inventory: writes inventory.yaml from the Terraform output
dns: checks that the apex, www and pma A records point at the instance
wait: waits up to 300 s for SSH

terraform.name: Terraform
terraform.description: Builds everything the playbook then configures, and tracks it in its state: a VPC with one public subnet, an internet gateway and route table, the cloud1-web security group, the cloud1-key key pair, the instance and its Elastic IP association.
facts: t3.micro running Ubuntu 22.04, encrypted 16 GB gp3 disk, IMDSv2 only
The Elastic IP is reserved in its own module (terraform/eip), so the DNS records survive a rebuild

ansible.name: Ansible
ansible.description: Connects to the instance over SSH as ubuntu and applies site.yml. It is idempotent: a second run reports changed=0. Secrets are encrypted with ansible-vault, and the vault password is never committed.
facts: Targets the webservers group in inventory.yaml
Renders docker-compose.yml to /opt/cloud1 and starts the stack
Issues the Let's Encrypt certificate with a one-shot certbot container

visitor.name: Visitor
visitor.description: Reaches the site by name. Both names resolve to the Elastic IP, and Nginx picks the virtual host from the Host header.

sg.name: Security group
sg.description: The first firewall, at the AWS edge, separate from ufw on the host. Opening a port in ufw is not enough: the security group must allow 22, 80 and 443 too, or AWS drops the packets before they reach the instance.
facts: Port 80 must stay open: Let's Encrypt validates the domain over HTTP-01

ufw.name: ufw
ufw.description: Set up by the security role: deny all incoming traffic, then allow only SSH, HTTP and HTTPS. The same role installs fail2ban and unattended upgrades, and hardens sshd.
facts: Default policy: deny incoming, allow outgoing
sshd: key-only login, no root login

nginx.name: Nginx
nginx.description: The only container that publishes ports. Port 80 answers with a 301 redirect to HTTPS (except the ACME challenge); port 443 terminates TLS 1.2/1.3 and routes by name. Unknown names get a 444.
facts: Image nginx:1.27-alpine, on the frontend network
Virtual hosts: youssefelhadraoui.tech, www and pma
Let's Encrypt certificate: a systemd timer checks it twice a day and renews it within 30 days of expiry; a self-signed one bootstraps the first start
Resolves the PHP upstreams per request through Docker's DNS (127.0.0.11)

wordpress.name: WordPress
wordpress.description: Publishes no ports: only Nginx reaches it, over FastCGI on port 9000. It reads and writes its data in MariaDB over the backend network.

phpmyadmin.name: phpMyAdmin
phpmyadmin.description: The database admin interface, served at pma.youssefelhadraoui.tech. Like WordPress, a php-fpm pool with no published ports.

mariadb.name: MariaDB
mariadb.description: Sits only on the backend network, declared internal: true, so it has no route off the host and stays unreachable from the internet, even if a port were published by mistake.
facts: Database wordpress, user wpuser, credentials from the vault
Named volume db_data, which survives reboots

iot.title: Inception-of-Things architecture
iot.description: Four parts, from a two-node K3s cluster on Vagrant to GitOps with Argo CD and a local Gitea. Pick a part, then explore its components.

p1.title: Part 1: K3s and Vagrant
p1.summary: Two Debian 12 Vagrant VMs on a VirtualBox private network form a two-node K3s cluster: a server (control plane) and an agent (worker).

vagrant.name: Vagrant
vagrant.description: Creates both VMs, sets their hostnames and private IPs, and runs the provisioning scripts. Both machines are reachable through passwordless vagrant ssh.
facts: vagrant up creates yelhadrS, then yelhadrSW
Each VM: 1 CPU and 1024 MB of RAM

server.name: yelhadrS
server.description: The control-plane node. setup_server.sh installs K3s in server mode, bound to the private network, with its API advertised on 192.168.56.110.
facts: Check: sudo kubectl get nodes -o wide

agent.name: yelhadrSW
agent.description: The worker node. setup_worker.sh waits until the server API answers, then installs K3s in agent mode and joins the cluster with the shared token.
facts: Retries the server API up to 120 times before giving up

p2.title: Part 2: K3s and three applications
p2.summary: One VM runs K3s in server mode. Traefik, the ingress controller bundled with K3s, routes each request to one of three apps based on its Host header.

client.name: curl
client.description: Sends requests to the VM's private IP with a Host header, for example curl -H "Host: app1.com" http://192.168.56.110.

traefik.name: Traefik
traefik.description: The apps-ingress Ingress (class traefik, entrypoint web) holds three rules: two host rules and a default rule with no host.

app1.name: app1
app1.description: A Deployment of nginxdemos/hello, a small page that shows which pod answered, behind the app1-svc Service.

app2.name: app2
app2.description: Same image with three replicas, as the subject requires; the Service spreads requests across the three pods.

app3.name: app3
app3.description: The default backend: any host other than app1.com or app2.com lands here.

p3.title: Part 3: K3d and Argo CD
p3.summary: K3d runs K3s inside Docker. Argo CD watches a public GitHub repository and keeps the dev namespace in sync with it: changing the image tag from v1 to v2 in Git updates the running app.

you.name: You
you.description: Changes the image tag in Git, then checks the result with curl.

github.name: GitHub
github.description: The source of truth: it holds the playground Deployment and Service, which Argo CD reads at HEAD from the repository root.

argocd.name: Argo CD
argocd.description: Installed from the upstream stable manifests. The playground Application syncs automatically, prunes deleted resources and reverts drift (selfHeal), so the cluster always matches Git.

playground.name: playground
playground.description: The application Argo CD deploys: one replica that answers on port 8888 with its version, v1 or v2.

lb.name: Load balancer
lb.description: k3d's load balancer maps a host port to the cluster, so localhost:8888 reaches the playground Service.

bonus.title: Bonus: local Gitea
bonus.summary: The same GitOps flow as Part 3, but the Git repository lives in a local Gitea, installed with Helm in its own namespace. Gitea replaces GitLab because it is much lighter on a laptop.

you.name: You
you.description: Edits the image tag in the Gitea web interface, then checks the app with curl.

lb.name: Load balancer
lb.description: k3d maps two host ports: 8081 to the cluster ingress on port 80, and 8888 to the playground LoadBalancer Service.

traefik.name: Traefik
traefik.description: The ingress controller bundled with K3s. The Gitea Helm chart creates an Ingress for gitea.localhost (class traefik).

gitea.name: Gitea
gitea.description: A lightweight Git server installed with the gitea-charts/gitea Helm chart. The setup script creates the playground repository and pushes the initial manifest (v1).
facts: Rootless image, SQLite, in-memory cache, SSH disabled
Admin account from the gitea-admin-secret Secret

argocd.name: Argo CD
argocd.description: Works as in Part 3, but its Application points at the in-cluster Gitea service instead of GitHub.
facts: Automated sync: prune, selfHeal; destination namespace dev

playground.name: playground
playground.description: The same application as in Part 3, now deployed from the local Gitea repository.
